Trite

TRYT -- one syllable, rhymes with 'bright.' · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Trite is overused and lacking originality.

Movie critics groaned at the film's trite ending, in which the hero wakes to find it was all a dream.

Worked Example

The new greeting-card writer drafts her first birthday line: 'Reach for the stars!' Her supervisor slides over a binder of cards from the last thirty years -- the exact phrase appears in more than two hundred of them.

'Reach for the stars' is trite: overused and lacking originality. Trite is aimed at LANGUAGE and ideas -- phrases, sayings, plot devices -- that once had force but have been repeated so many times they now land with no impact at all.

How Trite Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

hackneyed

hackneyed: made stale and dull by constant repetition

stale

stale: no longer fresh or interesting

worn-out

worn-out: used so often it has lost its force

Antonyms

fresh

fresh: new and original

original

original: invented newly, not copied

How Strong Is It? — stale → trite → hackneyed

stale vs. trite

stale vs. trite: Stale says the joke or phrase has simply lost its freshness, while trite adds a judgment: the expression was reached for lazily, because everyone always reaches for it.

hackneyed vs. trite

hackneyed vs. trite: Hackneyed is the strongest of the three: a trite line makes readers sigh, but a hackneyed one has been worked so hard for so long that critics treat using it as a small offense.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Trite comes straight from Latin tritus, 'rubbed away' -- the past participle of terere, 'to rub, to wear down.' A trite phrase is literally a worn one: handled so many times, like an old coin rubbed smooth, that its face has disappeared.

Use the root in a new word: attrition

Use the root in a new word: attrition: The club lost members to slow attrition, one quiet resignation at a time.

Root Check

Word Choice

Trite targets EXPRESSIONS and ideas: a trite phrase, trite dialogue, a trite moral, a trite plot twist. Keep it apart from its unit-mate banal -- banal covers broader dullness (a banal building, banal small talk), while trite specifically accuses language of being worn out through repetition. If it isn't words or an idea, banal is probably the better word.
